bhakra_dam.description: The Bhakra Dam on the Satluj river at the Himachal-Punjab border is a concrete gravity structure 226 m tall — among the higher gravity dams in the world at the time of its completion in 1963. Jawaharlal Nehru called it the 'New Temple of India', a phrase that captured the post-independence faith in large infrastructure as the instrument of national development. The Bhakra-Nangal project, which the dam anchors, irrigates 10 million hectares across Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan and produces 1,325 MW of power. Travellers can enter the dam area with a security permit obtainable at the gate; the view from the dam crest 210 m above the Satluj gorge is vertiginous. The engineering heritage of the dam and its associated infrastructure — the power houses, the railway, the township — is considerable.
bhakra_dam.name: Bhakra Dam

bilaspur_town.description: The current district headquarters of Bilaspur was built on higher ground above the reservoir shoreline after the submergence of old Bilaspur in 1963. The new town, planned in the 1950s, has the slightly incomplete character of a community built in anticipation rather than organically grown. The displaced families from the 360 submerged villages were resettled here and in Punjab, carrying with them the oral history and cultural memory of the drowned landscape. When the reservoir falls to extremely low levels in drought years, the ruins of the old Bilaspur fort, temples and roads briefly re-emerge from the water — ghostly appearances that draw the descendants of displaced families back to witness. The Vyas Cave shrine on a riverside promontory is one of the few ancient sites that survived above the waterline.
bilaspur_town.name: Bilaspur Town

dehar_hydro.description: The Dehar Power House on the Beas-Satluj Link Project, located where the diverted Beas water emerges from the 38 km trans-Himalayan tunnel at Sundernagar, is an underground power station buried within the hill — its turbines driven by a 430 m head of water from the Pandoh intake. The exterior of the facility is modest, but the engineering concept — the water travelling more than 38 km underground to drop 430 m and generate power — is extraordinary. The Dehar facility is not a tourist site per se, but the approach road along the Satluj between Bilaspur and Sundernagar passes through genuinely wild gorge country with good views of the river and the Shivalik formations.
dehar_hydro.name: Dehar Hydro

gobind_sagar_lake.description: India's fifth-largest man-made reservoir by water volume, Gobind Sagar was created in 1963 when the Bhakra Dam impounded the Satluj river, submerging the ancient town of Bilaspur, 360 villages and their temples beneath 168 km of water. The reservoir at full capacity stretches 90 km in length and covers 540 sq km — a vast inland sea ringed by Shivalik hills. Water sports including kayaking, water-skiing, speed boating and angling (mahseer and rohu are present in significant numbers) are organised from the Luhnu and Govind Sagar shoreline facilities. The lake changes character dramatically by season: blue and windswept in winter, green and still in pre-monsoon, and retreating to reveal red mud banks during the October drawdown. Fishing permits are available through the HP Fisheries Department.
gobind_sagar_lake.name: Gobind Sagar Lake

koldam_dam.description: The Koldam Hydroelectric Project on the Satluj river immediately upstream of Gobind Sagar was completed in 2021, making it one of India's newest large hydroelectric installations at 800 MW capacity. The reservoir behind the Koldam Dam occupies the narrow Satluj gorge above Sundernagar — a dramatically deep canyon where the river cuts through the Shivalik ridges. The dam site can be reached on the road between Mandi and Bilaspur, and the reservoir has already attracted winter waterfowl. The project's powerhouse is built underground within the gorge walls — an engineering approach that minimises surface impact.
koldam_dam.name: Koldam Dam

markand_temple.description: The Markand temple complex on the eastern shore of Gobind Sagar, accessible by boat from Bilaspur or by road via a rough track, is a 10th-century Shiva temple group that narrowly escaped submergence — the temples were located just above the full reservoir level. The carved stone panels on the temple exteriors, depicting Shiva, Vishnu, their consorts and celestial beings, are of considerable artistic quality and comparable to the best temple sculpture of the Pratihara period. The lakeside setting gives the complex a remarkably peaceful atmosphere, enhanced by the near-total absence of other visitors. Fishing from the temple ghats is done by locals on non-festival days.
markand_temple.name: Markand Temple

naina_devi_temple.description: At 1,219 m on a ridge that drops sharply 700 m into Gobind Sagar on three sides, the Naina Devi temple commands among the most spectacular positions of any religious site in Himachal Pradesh — the lake visible in three directions from the hilltop. Naina Devi is one of the 51 Shakti Peethas, marking where the eyes (nain) of the goddess Sati fell. The temple receives several million pilgrims annually, swelling enormously at Navratri. A ropeway from the base at Anandpur Sahib side provides access for those unable to climb the 1 km of steps. The adjacent Gobind Sagar viewpoint is a notable sunset observation points in the district, with the lake reflecting the fading light in extraordinary colour.
naina_devi_temple.name: Naina Devi Temple

nalwari_fair_ground.description: The Nalwari Mela, held annually in March at the Bilaspur Chaugan (town maidan), is one of the largest traditional cattle and livestock fairs in Himachal Pradesh — an event of considerable antiquity that historically served as the primary market for livestock trade between the hill communities and the plains buyers. While modern commercial livestock markets have reduced the scale of actual cattle trade, the fair has expanded as a cultural event with folk performances, food stalls, handicraft markets and agricultural equipment displays. The March timing coincides with the post-winter agricultural opening, and the fair has a distinctly festive atmosphere. The event runs for 3–5 days and draws tens of thousands of visitors.
nalwari_fair_ground.name: Nalwari Fair Ground

swarghat.description: Where the Satluj river enters Gobind Sagar at its northern end near Swarghat, the meeting of a fast mountain river with the still reservoir creates an exceptional landscape. The Satluj in its final gorge section above this point cuts through narrow sandstone cliffs that are coloured in bands of red, orange and buff — the characteristic Shivalik geological palette. A river beach at the confluence point is used for picnicking and casual fishing by local families. The Swarghat bridge on the Bilaspur-Mandi highway is a viewpoint for watching the Satluj emerge from its gorge. In October and November, when the reservoir is drawn down and the river is still running clear, the colour contrast between the blue-green river and the red cliffs is photogenic.
swarghat.name: Swarghat

vyas_gufa.description: On a rocky promontory above the Satluj river within Bilaspur town, the Vyas Gufa (Cave of Vyasa) is a natural cave associated with the legendary sage Vyas — credited with composing or assembling the Mahabharata and the Vedas. The cave has been a place of meditation for ascetics over many generations, and the current temple structure surrounding it has been maintained by a continuous succession of priests. The cave survived the Bhakra submergence because it sits above the full reservoir level. The Satluj gorge view from the cave entrance — the river 40 m below, the Gobind Sagar reservoir stretching south, and the Shivalik hills receding in every direction — is one of the district's finest viewpoints.
vyas_gufa.name: Vyas Gufa

sections.overview: Chamba is one of Himachal's most underrated districts. The old Chamba town has preserved ancient temples dating back 1,000+ years. Dalhousie, a former British cantonment, offers colonial charm and access to Dainkund Peak. Khajjiar is often described as the 'Mini Switzerland of India' — a circular meadow ringed by deodars with a small lake. The Ravi and Chenab rivers drain through this westernmost district.

bharmaur.description: At 2,130 m on the Budhil river, Bharmaur was the original capital of the Chamba kingdom for 400 years before Raja Sahil Varman moved the court to Chamba town in the 10th century. The Chaurasi (84) temple complex at its centre — a courtyard of 84 ancient shrines from the 7th to 10th centuries — ranks among the most significant ancient religious sites in the western Himalaya and yet receives only a trickle of visitors because of the difficult access. The main Manimahesh and Lakshmi Narayan temples in the Chaurasi complex are still active. Bharmaur is also the cultural and economic centre of the Gaddi tribe — the pastoral transhumant community whose shepherds take their flocks over 4,000 m passes between the Chamba winter pastures and the Lahaul summer meadows.
bharmaur.name: Bharmaur

chamba_town.description: The ancient capital of the Chamba kingdom, continuously settled for over 1,500 years, lies in a bend of the Ravi river at 996 m — unusually low for a Himachal town, giving it a warm, almost subtropical climate compared to the surrounding ranges. The Chaugan, a long open maidan in the town centre, is used for the Minjar Fair (August) — a week-long festival in which gods from 80+ surrounding villages are brought together in procession. The Lakshmi Narayan temple complex on the hillside above the Chaugan contains six stone shikharas from the 10th–19th centuries, the oldest being among the finest examples of the Pratihara architectural style in the western Himalaya. Chamba is also renowned for its Rumal — hand-embroidered silk cloth using a double-sided technique unique to the region.
chamba_town.name: Chamba Town

dainkund_peak.description: The highest accessible peak near Dalhousie at 2,755 m, Dainkund (sometimes called 'Singing Hill') is reached by a 2 km trail from the Dalhousie ridge that passes through meadows of wild strawberry and alpine herbs before reaching the rocky summit. The Pohlani Mata temple at the top is tended by a family of priests who live in the adjoining shelter throughout the year, even through heavy winter snowfall. The summit panorama takes in the Pir Panjal range to the north, the Ravi valley 1,000 m below, and on exceptionally clear winter mornings the plains of Punjab extending to the horizon. The Indian Air Force maintains an installation on the ridge below the summit.
dainkund_peak.name: Dainkund Peak

dalhousie.description: Built in the 1860s as a hill station for British troops who could not afford to summer in Shimla, Dalhousie spreads across five hills at an average altitude of 2,036 m in the Dhauladhar foothills. The cantonment character — churches, bungalows with verandas, pine-lined Mall roads — is better preserved here than in almost any other HP hill station, partly because the town never attracted significant industry or high-rise construction. Subhash Chowk, the main square, anchors the central ridge; the two Mall roads, Upper and Lower, offer forest walks with views toward the Pir Panjal on clear days. The writer Rabindranath Tagore and revolutionary Bhagat Singh both spent formative periods here. Dalhousie is cold and green in summer, snow-covered and scenic in winter.
dalhousie.name: Dalhousie

kalatop_wildlife_sanctuary.description: Between Dalhousie and Khajjiar, the 30 sq km Kalatop Sanctuary protects a notable surviving blocks of Himalayan moist temperate forest in the Chamba district — a dense canopy of deodar, silver fir, oak and rhododendron that receives snowfall for 3–4 months annually. The Kalatop Khajjiar Reserve contains black bear, leopard, yellow-throated marten, barking deer and over 100 bird species including the cheer pheasant (endangered). A forest rest house in the middle of the sanctuary offers basic accommodation bookable through the Forest Department — among the most atmospheric lodging experiences in Chamba. Walking trails through the sanctuary are open; a mandatory forest guard accompanies visits to the interior.
kalatop_wildlife_sanctuary.name: Kalatop Wildlife Sanctuary

khajjiar.description: Twenty-two km from Dalhousie through dense deodar forest, Khajjiar occupies a circular natural plateau of approximately 1.5 km diameter at 1,920 m — a bowl of short-cropped grass around a small lake, enclosed by an unbroken ring of mature deodar trees, so symmetrically scenic that it has been officially designated as one of 160 locations worldwide similar to Switzerland, earning the 'Mini Switzerland of India' title from the Swiss Ambassador in 1992. The Khajji Nag temple on the lake shore, dedicated to a serpent deity, is an ancient wooden structure predating the tourism. Horse riding, zorbing and paragliding are offered on the meadow. The sunset light through the deodars onto the lake is especially atmospheric.
khajjiar.name: Khajjiar

lakshmi_narayan_temple.description: The six-temple complex of Lakshmi Narayan in Chamba town represents the finest concentration of early medieval stone temple architecture in Himachal Pradesh. The oldest and largest temple, dedicated to Lakshmi Narayan (Vishnu), was built in the Shikhara style in the 10th century by Raja Sahil Varman, who is said to have diverted the Saho spring to bring water to the town. The stone carvings on the exterior walls — Vishnu in his ten avatars, Shiva with Parvati, celestial musicians and guardian figures — are of museum quality. Inside the temples, bronze castings and silver-repoussé panels from the 10th–17th centuries are displayed. The temples are active sites of worship and the priests are happy to explain the iconography.
lakshmi_narayan_temple.name: Lakshmi Narayan Temple

manimahesh_lake.description: At 4,080 m below the sacred peak of Manimahesh Kailash (5,653 m), this glacial lake is one of the holiest sites in Himachal Pradesh — Shiva is believed to reside on the mountain above, and the lake is considered his bathing pool. The annual Manimahesh Yatra (August–September, timed to the Radha Ashtami festival) brings up to 100,000 pilgrims along a 13 km trail from Hadsar, making it one of the Himalayas' great devotional journeys. Outside the yatra season the trail is almost empty and the landscape — moraines, alpine tundra, the dark lake and the white pyramid of Manimahesh — is strikingly austere. The approach road from Bharmour to Hadsar passes through the sacred Gaddi tribal homeland.
manimahesh_lake.name: Manimahesh Lake

pangi_valley.description: The Pangi Valley of the upper Chenab river is among the most isolated inhabited valleys in India — cut off by snow for five to six months annually, with road access only through the Sach Pass or the long route through Lahaul. The Pangwali people who inhabit Pangi's 40+ villages have a distinct culture, dialect and traditional costume that has been preserved by centuries of seasonal isolation. The valley receives almost no tourists outside the July–September window, and those who arrive find landscape of extraordinary severity: narrow gorges, rushing rapids and steep slopes with tiny terraced fields clinging to impossible angles. The Forest Department rest house at Kilar village is the only formal accommodation.
pangi_valley.name: Pangi Valley

sach_pass.description: At 4,390 m, the Sach Pass ranks among the most technically demanding high-altitude roads in India — a single-lane track carved into sheer rock faces above a 2,000 m void, crossing the Great Himalayan Range to link the Chamba Valley with the Pangi Valley. The road is unpaved, subject to landslides and snowfall from October to June, and passable only in 4WD vehicles with experienced drivers. The pass is flanked by permanent snowfields even in August, and the final approach involves river crossings and switchbacks of extreme gradient. This place is precisely this difficulty that makes the journey extraordinary: the view from the pass north into the Pangi valley is of a landscape that looks quite different from the better-known in the accessible parts of Himachal.
sach_pass.name: Sach Pass

The annual Manimahesh Yatra (August–September, timed to the Radha Ashtami festival) brings up to 100,000 pilgrims along a 13 km trail from Hadsar, making it one of the Himalayas' great devotional journeys. Outside the yatra season the trail is almost empty and the landscape — moraines, alpine tundra, the dark lake and the white pyramid of Manimahesh — is strikingly austere. The approach road from Bharmour to Hadsar passes through the sacred Gaddi tribal homeland.
manimahesh_lake.name: Manimahesh Lake

pangi_valley.description: The Pangi Valley of the upper Chenab river is among the most isolated inhabited valleys in India — cut off by snow for five to six months annually, with road access only through the Sach Pass or the long route through Lahaul. The Pangwali people who inhabit Pangi's 40+ villages have a distinct culture, dialect and traditional costume that has been preserved by centuries of seasonal isolation. The valley receives almost no tourists outside the July–September window, and those who arrive find landscape of extraordinary severity: narrow gorges, rushing rapids and steep slopes with tiny terraced fields clinging to impossible angles. The Forest Department rest house at Kilar village is the only formal accommodation.
pangi_valley.name: Pangi Valley

sach_pass.description: At 4,390 m, the Sach Pass ranks among the most technically demanding high-altitude roads in India — a single-lane track carved into sheer rock faces above a 2,000 m void, crossing the Great Himalayan Range to link the Chamba Valley with the Pangi Valley. The road is unpaved, subject to landslides and snowfall from October to June, and passable only in 4WD vehicles with experienced drivers. The pass is flanked by permanent snowfields even in August, and the final approach involves river crossings and switchbacks of extreme gradient. This place is precisely this difficulty that makes the journey extraordinary: the view from the pass north into the Pangi valley is of a landscape that looks quite different from the better-known in the accessible parts of Himachal.
sach_pass.name: Sach Pass

bhota.description: A river village on the left bank of the Beas between Hamirpur and the Dehra Gopipur bridge, Bhota is the site of a traditional market (haat) that has operated on fixed days for generations, drawing farmers from surrounding villages with seasonal produce. The Beas here flows through a wide gravel bed with good fishing for mahseer (the large carp of Himalayan rivers) in the pre-monsoon and post-monsoon windows. The riverside landscape with its poplar windbreaks, mustard fields and distant Dhauladhar backdrop is the quintessential lower Beas valley scene. Basic accommodation is available in the village for those wishing to base themselves here for river activities.

bijhari.description: A traditional Himachali village 8 km from Sujanpur Tira, Bijhari preserves examples of the vernacular domestic architecture of the lower Beas valley — two-storey stone-and-timber houses with carved woodwork, slate roofs and enclosed courtyards that are increasingly rare as concrete construction replaces traditional building. Homestay initiatives in several families here offer an immersive experience of Himachali agricultural and domestic life: participating in wheat harvest, learning to prepare local foods including siddu and madra, and accompanying the family's cattle to the forest pastures. The views toward the Dhauladhar from the village edge are excellent in clear winter weather.
bijhari.name: Bijhari

deotsidh_temple.description: On a forested ridge above the Beas river 12 km from Hamirpur town, the Deotsidh temple of Baba Balak Nath ranks among the most visited pilgrimage sites in the Punjab-Himachal belt — receiving an estimated 5–7 million visitors annually, predominantly from Punjab, Haryana and Delhi. Balak Nath is a child saint of the Nath tradition, believed to have meditated in the cave that now forms the inner sanctum of the temple. The cave shrine, where a naturally formed stalagmite is venerated as the saint's image, can be reached to devotees after a short climb on stone steps. The surrounding hillside now includes with gardens, dhaba facilities and pilgrim shelters. The Mela (fair) held on Sundays and on Navratri is particularly large.
deotsidh_temple.name: Deotsidh Temple

hamirpur_town.description: The district headquarters at 786 m is a compact, well-planned administrative town that reflects Hamirpur's status as the most literate district in Himachal Pradesh (literacy rate consistently above 88%). The National Institute of Technology Hamirpur, one of India's premier technical institutions, is headquartered here and gives the town a pronounced young and academic character. The town has little traditional heritage tourism value but serves as an efficient base for exploring Sujanpur Tira (18 km) and Deotsidh (12 km). The Hamirpur HRTC bus stand is one of the best-connected in the district, with direct services to Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala and Delhi.
hamirpur_town.name: Hamirpur Town

nadaun.description: On the banks of the Beas river 22 km east of Hamirpur, Nadaun is historically significant as the site of the Battle of Nadaun (1691) in which Guru Gobind Singh, allied with the Kangra hill rajas, defeated the Mughal forces of Alif Khan — an engagement documented in the Guru's autobiography, the Bachitar Natak. The Beas at Nadaun is wide and calm, with sand and gravel beaches that attract local visitors for bathing. The old ghats and the Nadaun fort ruins are evocative if fragmentary heritage sites. The town sits on the old caravan route from the Punjab plains to the Kullu Valley, and a weekly market (Monday) retains something of the traditional trading fair character.
nadaun.name: Nadaun

ranser_lake.description: A small reservoir on the edge of Hamirpur town created by damming the Ranser stream, this modest water body now includes as a recreational lake and picnic ground. Winter brings migratory waterfowl including bar-headed geese, pochards and various duck species to the lake — making it a surprisingly rewarding birdwatching site for a peri-urban location. The lake shore is planted with ornamental trees and has walking paths, a boating facility and seasonal food stalls. This place is primarily a local amenity but offers a pleasant hour of outdoor relaxation in combination with a visit to Hamirpur town.
ranser_lake.name: Ranser Lake

sujanpur_tira.description: Founded in 1748 by Raja Abhay Chand of the Kangra kingdom on a horseshoe bluff above the Beas river, Sujanpur Tira is a notable examples of an 18th-century planned Himalayan town — a grid of lanes centred on the fort complex with eight major temple complexes arranged around a large maidan. The town reached its cultural peak under the patronage of Raja Sansar Chand (1775–1823), who turned Sujanpur into a centre of Kangra miniature painting, music and drama. The Holi fair at Sujanpur (March) is the most celebrated festival in Hamirpur district, drawing participants for a week of music and colours on the riverside maidan. The ghats on the Beas below the fort are scenic at dawn.
sujanpur_tira.name: Sujanpur Tira

tarapur_fort.description: The fort at Sujanpur Tira, built by Raja Abhay Chand in 1748 and expanded by Raja Sansar Chand in the late 18th century, is formally often called Tarapur Fort — a reference to the local name for the bluff above the Beas. The fort's inner courts, now partially restored, display fragments of the Kangra-school wall paintings that once covered extensive interiors during Sansar Chand's reign. The fort commands an extensive view of the Beas valley, the Dhauladhar range to the north, and the Hamirpur–Kangra ridge to the south. The adjacent Narbadeshwar temple complex, with its multiple shrines from the 18th century, is active and scenicly maintained by local priests.
tarapur_fort.name: Tarapur Fort

dharamkot.description: A kilometre above McLeod Ganj on a forested spur, Dharamkot has evolved into Himachal's most concentrated centre for yoga, meditation and Vipassana practice. Dozens of centres offer courses ranging from drop-in yoga classes to month-long residential programmes in the Tibetan Buddhist, Vipassana, Kundalini and Ashtanga traditions. The village has strong cafes, a small traveller library and guesthouses in converted apple orchards. The trail to Triund begins here, and the short walk to the Guna Devi temple viewpoint offers the same Kangra Valley panorama without the full trek commitment. Dharamkot attracts a throughout the year community of long-stay international visitors seeking study and practice in an unhurried mountain setting.
dharamkot.name: Dharamkot

dharamshala___mcleod_ganj.description: Dharamshala is in fact two distinct towns separated by 500 m of altitude: lower Dharamshala, the administrative headquarters at 1,457 m; and McLeod Ganj (upper Dharamshala) at 1,457 m where the Central Tibetan Administration and the Dalai Lama's residence have been established since 1960. McLeod Ganj is a living expression of Tibetan civilisation in exile — the Namgyal Monastery, the Tibet Museum, the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, and dozens of meditation and yoga centres create a community that is simultaneously a spiritual destination and a political story. The surrounding landscape, with the Dhauladhar range rising sharply behind the town and the Kangra Valley spread below, is dramatic. The town is best visited March–May and October–November when the Dhauladhar is snow-capped and the monsoon or heat are not factors.
dharamshala___mcleod_ganj.name: Dharamshala / McLeod Ganj

kangra_fort.description: Rising on a rocky promontory at the confluence of the Baner and Majhi rivers, the Kangra Fort is one of the oldest forts in India — historical records place settlements on this site from the 3rd century BCE, and it was described by the armies of Mahmud of Ghazni in 1009 CE as the richest fort in Asia. The fort withstood repeated sieges before falling to the Mughal emperor Akbar in 1620; it was damaged irreparably by the 1905 Kangra earthquake. The ruined walls, towers and temple platforms still occupy an impressive area, with the Ambika Devi and Lakshmi Narayan temples inside the compound retaining their sanctity. The Archaeological Survey of India manages the site and has partially restored the entrance gateways.
kangra_fort.name: Kangra Fort

kareri_lake.description: A 14 km trail from Dharamshala winds through dense oak and rhododendron forest, crossing the Kareri stream multiple times on rope bridges and stepping stones before reaching this glacial lake at 2,950 m directly beneath the Dhauladhar's northern face. The lake freezes completely in winter and is surrounded by snow on its northern shore until late May. Trout have been introduced and the clear water supports a healthy population. Camping is permitted on the flat ground at the lake's eastern shore; basic food is available from a seasonal dhaba. The continuation trail climbs to the Minkiani Pass (4,350 m) for experienced trekkers with high-altitude gear. Kareri is a full-day excursion from Dharamshala or a more satisfying 2-day trip with a night camping at the lake.
kareri_lake.name: Kareri Lake

masrur_rock_cut_temple.description: Carved in the early 8th century from a single massive sandstone outcrop in the Beas valley, the Masrur temples are among the most remarkable and least-visited heritage sites in northern India — a group of 15 interconnected shikharas cut directly into a natural hillside in the late Pratihara style. Partially destroyed by the 1905 earthquake and never fully excavated, the temples contain carved panels of Shiva, Vishnu and their attendants of considerable artistic refinement. The reservoir created below the rock reflects The temple site at sunset, creating a photographic composition particularly scenic. Masrur is often compared to the Ellora caves and sometimes called 'the Kangra Khajuraho'; This place is inexplicably absent from most tourist itineraries.
masrur_rock_cut_temple.name: Masrur Rock Cut Temple

palampur.description: At 1,220 m on the lower slopes of the Dhauladhar, Palampur is Himachal Pradesh's tea capital — the only significant tea-growing region in the state, established by British planters in the 1860s using bushes brought from Darjeeling. The vivid green of the tea terraces against the snow backdrop of the Dhauladhar is a striking landscape. Neugal Khad, a narrow gorge carved by the Neugal stream just west of town, is a dramatic viewpoint and picnic site. Tashijong monastery, 5 km south, is a major Drukpa Kagyu centre with scenic wall paintings and a traditional crafts workshop. The town has well-maintained colonial-era buildings and is a useful base for exploring both the lower Kangra Valley and the Billing paragliding site.
palampur.name: Palampur

triund_trek.description: The Triund ridge (2,828 m) is accessed by a 9 km trail from McLeod Ganj that ascends through oak and rhododendron forest before emerging on a long grassy ridge directly beneath the Dhauladhar's vertical rock face. The contrast is abrupt and spectacular: the trail that passes through dense forest delivers walkers without warning to an open meadow with a sheer 1,500 m cliff rising immediately behind and the entire Kangra Valley spread 1,400 m below. The trek takes 3–4 hours ascending, 2–3 hours descending, and is suitable for reasonably fit walkers. Overnight camping on the ridge, in tents rented from Gaddi shepherd families, transforms the experience — dawn light on the Dhauladhar is memorable. The Snow Line Café at the ridge serves chai and dal; beyond it, the trail continues to Lahesh Cave and the Indrahar Pass (4,342 m).
triund_trek.name: Triund Trek

kareri_lake.description: A 14 km trail from Dharamshala winds through dense oak and rhododendron forest, crossing the Kareri stream multiple times on rope bridges and stepping stones before reaching this glacial lake at 2,950 m directly beneath the Dhauladhar's northern face. The lake freezes completely in winter and is surrounded by snow on its northern shore until late May. Trout have been introduced and the clear water supports a healthy population. Camping is permitted on the flat ground at the lake's eastern shore; basic food is available from a seasonal dhaba. The continuation trail climbs to the Minkiani Pass (4,350 m) for experienced trekkers with high-altitude gear. Kareri is a full-day excursion from Dharamshala or a more satisfying 2-day trip with a night camping at the lake.
kareri_lake.name: Kareri Lake

masrur_rock_cut_temple.description: Carved in the early 8th century from a single massive sandstone outcrop in the Beas valley, the Masrur temples are among the most remarkable and least-visited heritage sites in northern India — a group of 15 interconnected shikharas cut directly into a natural hillside in the late Pratihara style. Partially destroyed by the 1905 earthquake and never fully excavated, the temples contain carved panels of Shiva, Vishnu and their attendants of considerable artistic refinement. The reservoir created below the rock reflects The temple site at sunset, creating a photographic composition particularly scenic. Masrur is often compared to the Ellora caves and sometimes called 'the Kangra Khajuraho'; This place is inexplicably absent from most tourist itineraries.
masrur_rock_cut_temple.name: Masrur Rock Cut Temple

palampur.description: At 1,220 m on the lower slopes of the Dhauladhar, Palampur is Himachal Pradesh's tea capital — the only significant tea-growing region in the state, established by British planters in the 1860s using bushes brought from Darjeeling. The vivid green of the tea terraces against the snow backdrop of the Dhauladhar is a striking landscape. Neugal Khad, a narrow gorge carved by the Neugal stream just west of town, is a dramatic viewpoint and picnic site. Tashijong monastery, 5 km south, is a major Drukpa Kagyu centre with scenic wall paintings and a traditional crafts workshop. The town has well-maintained colonial-era buildings and is a useful base for exploring both the lower Kangra Valley and the Billing paragliding site.
palampur.name: Palampur

triund_trek.description: The Triund ridge (2,828 m) is accessed by a 9 km trail from McLeod Ganj that ascends through oak and rhododendron forest before emerging on a long grassy ridge directly beneath the Dhauladhar's vertical rock face. The contrast is abrupt and spectacular: the trail that passes through dense forest delivers walkers without warning to an open meadow with a sheer 1,500 m cliff rising immediately behind and the entire Kangra Valley spread 1,400 m below. The trek takes 3–4 hours ascending, 2–3 hours descending, and is suitable for reasonably fit walkers. Overnight camping on the ridge, in tents rented from Gaddi shepherd families, transforms the experience — dawn light on the Dhauladhar is memorable. The Snow Line Café at the ridge serves chai and dal; beyond it, the trail continues to Lahesh Cave and the Indrahar Pass (4,342 m).
triund_trek.name: Triund Trek

chitkul.description: At 3,450 m on the Baspa river, Chitkul is the last inhabited village on the Indo-Tibetan Border Road — the formal end of the tourist zone before restricted territory begins. The village is exceptionally well preserved: the traditional Kinnauri wooden architecture, the ancient Mathi temple with its silver-plated deity, and the setting against a cirque of glaciated peaks above the valley head create a scene that feels genuinely remote even at peak season. Midsummer brings alpine flowers to the pastures above the village; the upper meadows are accessible on a 3–4 hour walk. Camping is permitted in the flat ground near the river, and basic guesthouses in village homes offer authentic hospitality. The potato fields of Chitkul supply seed potatoes to Punjab.
chitkul.name: Chitkul

hangrang_valley.description: The innermost sub-division of Kinnaur, Hangrang (also spelled Hangrang) is a restricted zone requiring an Inner Line Permit — a requirement that has preserved its extraordinary cultural and landscape integrity. The valley, draining to the Satluj near Puh at 2,300 m, contains the ancient villages of Nako, Chango, Sumdo and Khab — each with its own monastery, dialect variation and traditional textile tradition. The Khab confluence, where the Spiti river meets the Satluj, ranks among the most dramatic landscape moments in the Indian Himalaya: two rivers of entirely different colour joining in a gorge of near-vertical rock walls. The region sees fewer than 5,000 visitors annually, making it among the most genuinely remote accessible valleys in India.
hangrang_valley.name: Hangrang Valley

kalpa.description: Set at 2,960 m on a forested terrace above the Satluj gorge, Kalpa offers what many photographers consider the finest mountain vista in Himachal Pradesh: the six-summited Kinnaur Kailash massif (6,050 m) rising directly behind the village, close enough that the rock changes colour visibly through the day from pre-dawn grey through amber sunrise to the blue-white of full daylight. The village is a tightly packed cluster of traditional three-storey Kinnauri homes with carved wooden windows and prayer-flag lines, interspersed with apricot and apple orchards. The ancient Hu-Bu-Lan-Kar temple complex in the lower village preserves Buddhist and Hindu iconography in the syncretic Kinnauri tradition. Kalpa is best visited October–November during the apple harvest.
kalpa.name: Kalpa

kamru_fort.description: Rising on a rocky spur directly above Sangla village, the Kamru Fort is a 7-storey wooden and stone tower — the former seat of the Bushahr kings before they moved to Rampur. Each storey is progressively smaller, creating a pagoda-like silhouette that is the defining image of the Sangla valley. Inside, the fort houses the Kamakhya Devi temple with a silver-faced goddess idol of considerable antiquity; non-Hindus must leave footwear and leather at the gate. The climb to the fort through the old village lanes passes traditional Kinnauri homes with carved wooden balconies. The view from the fort roof over the orchard valley to the snow peaks beyond is exceptional on clear October mornings.
kamru_fort.name: Kamru Fort

lippa-asrang_sanctuary.description: This 30 sq km wildlife sanctuary on the mid-elevation slopes of the Kinnaur district protects a transitional forest zone between the sub-alpine oak-conifer belt and the high-altitude scrub — a habitat that supports snow leopard, Himalayan black bear, musk deer and the koklass pheasant. The sanctuary is not set up for formal wildlife tourism and has no visitor facilities, but local naturalists in Sangla can arrange guided walks on the sanctuary margins in spring and autumn. The Lippa village on the sanctuary edge is noted for its production of Kinnauri shawls — handwoven wool and pashmina textiles with the distinctive geometric border pattern. The forest is particularly scenic in October when the broad-leafed trees turn amber and red against the dark conifers.
lippa-asrang_sanctuary.name: Lippa-Asrang Sanctuary

nako.description: High above the Satluj gorge at 3,662 m, Nako is a cluster of whitewashed homes around a sacred Buddhist lake — among the most atmospherically situated villages in the district. The Nako monastery complex, dating to the 10th century, contains some of the oldest surviving Buddhist murals in the Kinnaur-Spiti corridor. The sacred lake, around which locals walk in circumambulation (parikrama), mirrors the sky with perfect clarity at dawn. The surrounding landscape is characteristic of the rain-shadow Kinnaur — arid brown hills streaked with mineral colour, in sharp contrast to the green terraced fields irrigated from the village spring. Nako sits on the old trade route to Tibet and retains a strong Tibetan cultural character.
nako.name: Nako

reckong_peo.description: The district headquarters of Kinnaur at 2,670 m, Reckong Peo is the administrative centre where Inner Line Permits for restricted areas are issued, making it an essential stop for travellers heading to Hangrang Valley, Nako, or Puh. The town is a grid of government offices, a busy bazaar and a large Buddhist monastery with views across the Satluj gorge to the Kinnaur Kailash range. The weekly market (Thursday) is a cultural hub drawing traders from remote villages. The Kothi apple orchards below town are among the finest in the district. The road north from Reckong Peo to Kalpa (7 km) ranks among the most dramatic short drives in Himachal, hugging a cliff face above a 1,500 m gorge.
reckong_peo.name: Reckong Peo

sangla_valley.description: The Baspa river valley, accessed from the Hindustan-Tibet Highway at Karcham, ranks among the most scenic sub-valleys in all of Himachal Pradesh — a 20 km corridor of orchards, meadows and traditional villages backed by Himalayan peaks. Sangla village at 2,680 m is the valley's main settlement, with guesthouses, a weekly market, and the distinctive Kamru Fort rising above the rooftops. The valley narrows progressively as it ascends to Chitkul, with the Baspa running green and fast alongside the road. Apple, apricot and walnut orchards line the valley floor; in autumn (September–October) the combined colour of ripening fruit and turning deciduous trees makes the Sangla valley arguably the most photogenic landscape in Kinnaur.
sangla_valley.name: Sangla Valley

tabo.description: Shared between Kinnaur and Spiti sub-divisions, Tabo's monastery complex founded in 996 CE by the great translator Rinchen Zangpo is the crown jewel of Buddhist heritage in the western Himalayas. The nine temples of the 'Ajanta of the Himalayas' contain clay sculptures and fresco cycles of extraordinary refinement, depicting Buddhas, bodhisattvas and mandalas in the Kashmiri style that influenced Buddhist art across the Himalayan region. The village at 3,050 m is warmer and more sheltered than Kaza, and the apple orchards and poplar groves around it are productive. Two caves in the cliff above the monastery were used by meditating monks over many generations; one is still occasionally occupied. The annual Tabo festival (June) draws monks from across the Tibetan Buddhist world.
tabo.name: Tabo

sections.overview: Kullu district is the adventure capital of Himachal Pradesh. The Kullu Valley, carved by the Beas river, stretches from Larji gorge in the south to the Rohtang Pass in the north. Manali, its most famous town, is the gateway to Leh-Ladakh and Spiti. The district is best known for the Kullu Dussehra festival — one of India's most spectacular — and for world-class trekking, skiing, river rafting and paragliding.

atal_tunnel_viewpoint.description: The Atal Tunnel, inaugurated in 2020 at 3,000 m under the Pir Panjal range, is the world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet, cutting the Manali–Keylong drive from 4-5 hours to under 1 by bypassing the Rohtang Pass. The South Portal near Manali has become a destination in its own right, with viewpoints over the Solang and Beas valleys, snow-play areas in season, and stalls selling hot food to travellers before the 9.02 km crossing into Lahaul. It has fundamentally reshaped access to Spiti and Ladakh, keeping the route open for several extra months a year.
atal_tunnel_viewpoint.name: Atal Tunnel Viewpoint

bahu_village.description: Bahu is a quiet apple-orchard village in the Kullu valley, largely untouched by the tourist traffic of nearby Manali. Traditional Kullui slate-roofed houses sit among terraced orchards with views across the Beas valley, and the village makes a peaceful base for short walks rather than a marquee sightseeing stop — the appeal here is the ordinary rhythm of valley life.
bahu_village.name: Bahu Village

bijli_mahadev.description: Perched at 2,460 m above the Kullu valley, Bijli Mahadev temple houses a 60-foot stone Shiva lingam said to be struck by lightning periodically; local tradition holds that the priest repairs the shattered lingam each time using butter and grain, which is believed to make it whole again. Reaching the temple requires a steep 3 km climb from the roadhead at Chansari, rewarded with a 360-degree panorama of the Kullu and Parvati valleys meeting at Bhuntar.
bijli_mahadev.name: Bijli Mahadev

chalal.description: Chalal sits across the Parvati river from Kasol, reachable only on foot via a forest and riverside trail (no road access), which keeps it quieter than its neighbour. The short walk passes waterfalls and dense pine cover, and the village itself has become a small backpacker stop with cafes, functioning as a gentler alternative or first stage before the longer Kheerganga trek.
chalal.name: Chalal

chandrakhani_pass.description: The Chandrakhani Pass (3,660 m) trek begins in Naggar and crosses a high ridge before descending into the Malana village — home of the famously isolated Malana people who claim descent from Alexander the Great's soldiers. The two-day route passes through oak and rhododendron forest on the ascent, then across alpine meadows carpeted in summer wildflowers on approach to the pass. From the top, views extend to Deo Tibba (6,001 m) and the Hanuman Tibba massif, with the Kullu Valley 2,000 m below. Malana is a restricted village — visitors may not touch buildings or residents, and photography requires discretion.
chandrakhani_pass.name: Chandrakhani Pass

great_himalayan_national_park.description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014, the Great Himalayan National Park spans over 1,170 sq km of the western Himalaya in the upper Sainj, Tirthan and Jiwa valleys, protecting snow leopard, Himalayan tahr, musk deer and over 180 bird species across alpine meadows, glaciers and temperate forest. Entry requires permits from the park office at Sai Ropa, and multi-day treks (guides mandatory beyond the buffer zone) reach remote high-altitude pastures rarely visited outside dedicated wildlife and trekking circuits.
great_himalayan_national_park.name: Great Himalayan National Park

hadimba_temple.description: Built in 1553 in a cedar forest above Old Manali, the four-tiered pagoda-style Hadimba Devi Temple is dedicated to Hadimba from the Mahabharata, wife of Bhima, and is among Himachal's most distinctive wooden temples, with elaborately carved doorways and animal-horn trophies fixed to its walls. The surrounding Dhungri deodar forest, some trees centuries old, is as much a draw as the temple itself, and the annual Dhungri Mela in May is a major local festival.
hadimba_temple.name: Hadimba Temple

jalori_pass.description: At 3,120 m, Jalori Pass connects the Kullu valley to the Anni-Banjar side of the district and the Sainj/Tirthan valleys beyond, framed by dense oak and deodar forest. It's a popular base for short treks to Serolsar Lake (5 km) and longer routes toward Raghupur Fort, and the pass itself is usually snowbound December–March, reopening by road around April.
jalori_pass.name: Jalori Pass

jana_waterfall.description: A multi-tiered waterfall near Jana village on the way to Naggar, reached by a short forested walk from the road. Less commercialised than Kullu's better-known falls, it draws mostly local day-trippers and travellers combining it with visits to Naggar Castle and the Roerich Art Gallery nearby.
jana_waterfall.name: Jana Waterfall

jibhi.description: Tucked into the Banjar sub-valley off the main Kullu highway, Jibhi became a word-of-mouth traveller discovery after 2015 and has since blossomed into one of Himachal's finest slow-travel villages. A wooden bridge over a clear stream, traditional Himachali houses with carved balconies, and a backdrop of fir and cedar-clad ridges frame a landscape that feels genuinely timeless. The Jalori Pass (3,120 m) is a 14 km drive away, opening a trail network to Serolsar Lake and the Raghupur Fort ruins. Staying in a heritage homestay here over two or three nights rewards patient visitors with evening light that turns the forest gold.
jibhi.name: Jibhi

kalga.description: Kalga is a traditional wood-and-stone Himachali village on the slopes above the Parvati valley, past Barshaini, and has become a favoured stop for slow-travel backpackers for its terraced fields, apple orchards and views toward the snowline. It's a common base or first night for treks toward Kheerganga and Tosh, quieter and less developed than the villages lower in the valley.
kalga.name: Kalga

kasol.description: Set in the narrow inner gorge of the Parvati Valley where the Kasol stream meets the Parvati river, this small village at 1,640 m has evolved from a single guesthouse in the 1980s into the most internationally known backpacker hub in the Indian Himalayas. Israeli travellers, who nicknamed it 'Little Israel', established a culture of long stays, quality café food and river-side relaxation that persists today. The village is the trailhead for the Kheerganga trek and a staging point for longer wilderness routes into Pin-Parvati Pass. Best visited October–November or March–May when the valley is clear and the waterfalls above the village are running full.
kasol.name: Kasol

kheerganga.description: The 13 km trail from Barshaini climbs through pine and birch forest, passes the rock-face waterfall at Rudra Nag, and emerges above the treeline at Kheerganga's high meadow at 2,960 m — a journey that rewards effort with one of Himachal's most satisfying overnight experiences. A natural hot spring pool at the top, maintained by the Forest Department, allows tired trekkers to soak under open sky with views of the Parvati glacier above. The flat camping ground is large and well-organised, with basic dhabas serving chai and dal. The descent on the same trail takes 3.5–4 hours and is best done before midday to avoid afternoon cloud.
kheerganga.name: Kheerganga

kullu.description: The district headquarters on the banks of the Beas river, Kullu town is the traditional gateway to the valley and best known for the Kullu Dussehra, a week-long festival (unlike the rest of India, celebrated after Dussehra elsewhere) where over 200 local deities are carried in procession to the Dhalpur maidan. The town is also a base for river rafting on the Beas and a hub for the region's famous woollen shawls and caps, sold widely along its bazaar.
kullu.name: Kullu Town

malana.description: Isolated in a valley below Chandrakhani Pass, Malana is one of the Himalayas' most distinctive villages, with its own language (Kanashi), a self-governing council system centred on the local deity Jamlu Devta, and customs that discourage outsiders from touching village buildings or residents. Reached by trek from Jari, it's a place to visit with awareness and respect for local rules rather than as a casual sightseeing stop.
malana.name: Malana Village

manali.description: Perched at 2,050 m where the Beas river cuts through dense deodar forests, Manali is the anchor of all Kullu Valley travel. The old bazaar on Mall Road buzzes throughout the year with trekkers, honeymooners and bikers preparing for the Leh highway. The river banks at Van Vihar and the apple orchards of Kullu provide a quieter counterpoint to the tourist strip. In winter, snowfall transforms the town into a cosy alpine retreat with rooftop cafes and open fires.
manali.name: Manali

manikaran_sahib.description: Manikaran is a major pilgrimage site for both Sikhs and Hindus, home to a large Sikh gurudwara and a Ram temple built around natural sulphur hot springs said in Sikh tradition to have appeared at Guru Nanak's visit. The springs are hot enough that the gurudwara kitchen cooks langar meals in cloth pouches lowered into the water, and free hot-spring baths (separate for men and women) draw pilgrims and travellers combining a stop here with the Parvati valley trekking circuit.
manikaran_sahib.name: Manikaran Sahib

naggar.description: The former capital of the Kullu kingdom for over 1,400 years, Naggar sits on a forested terrace above the left bank of the Beas with views across to the snow peaks above Rohtang. Naggar Castle — a fine example of the Katoch style of timber-and-stone construction — was built in the 15th century and is now a heritage hotel and museum. The Russian artist Nicholas Roerich lived here from 1929 until his death in 1947; his estate, the Roerich Art Gallery, preserves his extraordinary paintings of the Himalayan landscape. The temple of Tripura Sundari, with its pagoda-style wooden tower, is a notable examples of Himachali religious architecture in the valley.
naggar.name: Naggar

old_manali.description: Separated from the main town by the Manalsu stream, Old Manali feels like a different world — a village of slate-roofed stone houses, apple trees and prayer flags. The ancient Manu Maharishi temple, said to mark where the sage Manu survived the great flood, sits at the top of the village on a wooden shikhara platform. The lane from the bridge up to the temple is lined with guesthouses and cafes that have made Old Manali a favourite slow-travel base since the 1980s. Best explored on foot in the early morning before the day-trippers arrive.
old_manali.name: Old Manali

pulga.description: A short walk past Barshaini and neighbouring Kalga, Pulga is a small terraced-field village on the Kheerganga trekking route, known for its slower pace, guesthouses run out of traditional homes, and views down the Parvati valley. It's a common overnight stop for trekkers pacing the climb to Kheerganga over two easier days rather than one long push.
pulga.name: Pulga

raison.description: A stretch of riverside meadow on the Beas between Kullu and Manali, Raison is best known for its HPTDC-run camping ground and as a put-in/take-out point for Beas river rafting runs. Its position roughly midway along the valley makes it a convenient stop for a short break or overnight camp away from the busier towns.
raison.name: Raison

rohtang_pass.description: The Rohtang Pass (4,111 m) functions as the great gateway of Lahaul — the point at which the monsoon-fed green world of the Kullu Valley abruptly gives way to the rain-shadow landscapes of Lahaul and ultimately Spiti. For Lahaul, Rohtang is not a visitor attraction but a lifeline: the pass closes from November to May under heavy snowfall, cutting Lahaul off from Manali and the outside world until the Atal Tunnel (opened 2020) changed the equation throughout the year. The approach from the Lahaul (northern) side is gentler than the Kullu face, passing the Chandra river headwaters and the vast flat Lahaul valley dotted with poplar trees and whitewashed gompas. The Atal Rohtang Tunnel at 3,100 m is now the practical route; the pass itself is visited as an excursion from Manali.
rohtang_pass.name: Rohtang Pass

sainj_valley.description: One of the entry points to the Great Himalayan National Park, Sainj Valley is a quieter, less-visited counterpart to the Tirthan valley next door, with terraced fields, apple orchards and the Sainj river running through pine and deodar forest. It functions mainly as a base for park treks and birdwatching rather than a standalone tourist stop.
sainj_valley.name: Sainj Valley

serolsar_lake.description: A small, still lake at around 3,100 m reached by a roughly 5 km forest walk from Jalori Pass, Serolsar is considered sacred to the local goddess Budhi Nagin, whose shrine sits at the water's edge. The trail through dense oak forest is a popular easy-to-moderate day trek, often paired with a visit to Jalori Pass itself.
serolsar_lake.name: Serolsar Lake

shoja.description: A small village just below Jalori Pass on the Banjar side, Shoja has good views over the Banjar and Tirthan valleys and has grown as a low-key alternative base to Manali for travellers heading toward Jalori Pass, Serolsar Lake or the Great Himalayan National Park, without the crowds of the main Kullu valley.
shoja.name: Shoja

solang_valley.description: A broad glacial valley 14 km north of Manali, Solang is Himachal's most versatile adventure corridor. In winter (January–March) it becomes a skiing and snowboarding destination with a rope tow and ski school; in summer, paragliding launches from the upper meadows and a gondola cable car carries visitors to 2,480 m for views of the Beas Kund glacier. The valley floor has a string of dhabas and equipment rental shops, and the drive up alongside the Solang stream through silver birch groves is scenic in its own right.
solang_valley.name: Solang Valley

tirthan_valley.description: The Tirthan river — cold, fast and impossibly clear — defines this valley that forms the buffer zone of the Great Himalayan National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Trails into the core zone of the national park require a registered guide and pass through rhododendron, oak and conifer forest that shelters Himalayan tahr, serow and the elusive snow leopard at higher elevations. Village homestays run by local families are among the most authentic accommodation experiences in Himachal.
tirthan_valley.name: Tirthan Valley

tosh.description: The last motorable-adjacent village at the head of the Parvati valley (a short walk from the road end at Barshaini), Tosh has grown from a quiet apple-farming hamlet into one of the valley's most popular backpacker stops, known for wooden-house guesthouses stacked up the hillside, valley views, and its position as a base for further treks toward Kheerganga and beyond.
tosh.name: Tosh

vashisht_hot_springs.description: A short climb above Manali, Vashisht village has natural sulphur hot-spring baths housed within an old stone temple complex dedicated to sage Vashisht, alongside a separate Ram temple in wood-carved Kullu style. The village itself has developed into a compact café and guesthouse hub popular with longer-staying travellers, distinct in character from the busier main Manali strip below.
vashisht_hot_springs.name: Vashisht Hot Springs

kullu.description: Kullu district is the adventure capital of Himachal Pradesh. The Kullu Valley, carved by the Beas river, stretches from Larji gorge in the south to the Rohtang Pass in the north. Manali, its most famous town, is the gateway to Leh-Ladakh and Spiti. The district is best known for the Kullu Dussehra festival — one of India's most spectacular — and for world-class trekking, skiing, river rafting and paragliding.

kullu.name: KULLU

chandrakhani_pass.description: The Chandrakhani Pass (3,660 m) trek begins in Naggar and crosses a high ridge before descending into the Malana village — home of the famously isolated Malana people who claim descent from Alexander the Great's soldiers. The two-day route passes through oak and rhododendron forest on the ascent, then across alpine meadows carpeted in summer wildflowers on approach to the pass. From the top, views extend to Deo Tibba (6,001 m) and the Hanuman Tibba massif, with the Kullu Valley 2,000 m below. Malana is a restricted village — visitors may not touch buildings or residents, and photography requires discretion.
chandrakhani_pass.name: Chandrakhani Pass

jibhi.description: Tucked into the Banjar sub-valley off the main Kullu highway, Jibhi became a word-of-mouth traveller discovery after 2015 and has since blossomed into one of Himachal's finest slow-travel villages. A wooden bridge over a clear stream, traditional Himachali houses with carved balconies, and a backdrop of fir and cedar-clad ridges frame a landscape that feels genuinely timeless. The Jalori Pass (3,120 m) is a 14 km drive away, opening a trail network to Serolsar Lake and the Raghupur Fort ruins. Staying in a heritage homestay here over two or three nights rewards patient visitors with evening light that turns the forest gold.

kasol.description: Set in the narrow inner gorge of the Parvati Valley where the Kasol stream meets the Parvati river, this small village at 1,640 m has evolved from a single guesthouse in the 1980s into the most internationally known backpacker hub in the Indian Himalayas. Israeli travellers, who nicknamed it 'Little Israel', established a culture of long stays, quality café food and river-side relaxation that persists today. The village is the trailhead for the Kheerganga trek and a staging point for longer wilderness routes into Pin-Parvati Pass. Best visited October–November or March–May when the valley is clear and the waterfalls above the village are running full.
kasol.name: Kasol

kheerganga.description: The 13 km trail from Barshaini climbs through pine and birch forest, passes the rock-face waterfall at Rudra Nag, and emerges above the treeline at Kheerganga's high meadow at 2,960 m — a journey that rewards effort with one of Himachal's most satisfying overnight experiences. A natural hot spring pool at the top, maintained by the Forest Department, allows tired trekkers to soak under open sky with views of the Parvati glacier above. The flat camping ground is large and well-organised, with basic dhabas serving chai and dal. The descent on the same trail takes 3.5–4 hours and is best done before midday to avoid afternoon cloud.

manali.description: Perched at 2,050 m where the Beas river cuts through dense deodar forests, Manali is the anchor of all Kullu Valley travel. The old bazaar on Mall Road buzzes throughout the year with trekkers, honeymooners and bikers preparing for the Leh highway. The river banks at Van Vihar and the apple orchards of Kullu provide a quieter counterpoint to the tourist strip. In winter, snowfall transforms the town into a cosy alpine retreat with rooftop cafes and open fires.

Naggar Castle — a fine example of the Katoch style of timber-and-stone construction — was built in the 15th century and is now a heritage hotel and museum. The Russian artist Nicholas Roerich lived here from 1929 until his death in 1947; his estate, the Roerich Art Gallery, preserves his extraordinary paintings of the Himalayan landscape. The temple of Tripura Sundari, with its pagoda-style wooden tower, is a notable examples of Himachali religious architecture in the valley.

The Sukhet kingdom was an independent polity that controlled central Mandi before being absorbed by the Mandi rajas in the 18th century. The fort views over the Beas valley and toward the Dhauladhar are excellent. A small temple on the summit ridge is still active. The climb from the base village takes approximately 45 minutes on a rough trail through scrub forest.
kamlah_fort.name: Kamlah Fort

karsog.description: Hidden in a broad sub-valley of the Satluj system south of the main Mandi-Shimla highway, Karsog at 1,400 m is one of the least-visited valley settlements in Mandi district — a landscape of terraced rice fields, apple orchards and deodar forest with a distinctly traditional Himachali character. The apple harvest (September–October) is the best time to visit; the orchards around Karsog produce a unique 'Karsog apple' variety prized for its flavour. A handful of basic guesthouses and homestays accommodate the occasional traveller who takes the 40 km detour from the main highway.

mandi_town.description: Seated at the confluence of the Uhl and Beas rivers at 760 m, Mandi is often described as the 'Varanasi of the Hills' — a title earned by the extraordinary density of temples in and around the old city: over 81 ancient stone temples, many dating to the 16th–18th century Sena dynasty, are documented within the town and its immediate surroundings. The ghats on the Beas, the Trilokinath temple (17th century), and the series of temples along the old bazaar lanes create a genuinely devotional townscape. The Mandi Shivratri fair (February–March) brings over 200 gods from surrounding villages to the Chaugan maidan in palanquins for a week of processions, music and commerce — one of Himachal's most significant cultural events. The Raj Mahal palace (1925) on the riverside is now a heritage hotel.
mandi_town.name: Mandi Town

pandoh_dam.description: The Pandoh Dam on the Beas river, 15 km south of Kullu town, is the intake structure of the Beas-Satluj Link Project — a major engineering achievement that diverts Beas water through a 38 km tunnel under the Dhauladhar to the Satluj at Sundernagar. The reservoir created behind the dam fills a narrow gorge with exceptionally clear green water, flanked by near-vertical cliff faces. A viewpoint and picnic area on the dam top attracts local visitors. The road on the south bank of the reservoir, bypassed by the main NH3 highway, is a scenic alternative with fine views of the water in the gorge. The dam has eliminated the spring floods that historically devastated the lower Beas valley.

The three-storey wooden pagoda temple on the lake shore, built in the 13th century without nails using the traditional Himachali interlocking joint technique, is a masterwork of regional architecture. Camping on the ridge above the lake under a sky dense with stars is a defining experience of the district.
prashar_lake.name: Prashar Lake

rewalsar_lake.description: Compressed within the Shivalik hills south of Mandi at 1,360 m, Rewalsar ranks among the most spiritually complex sites in India — a single lake simultaneously sacred to three distinct religious traditions. Buddhists revere it as the place where Guru Padmasambhava (Rinpoche), founder of Tibetan Buddhism, meditated before departing for Tibet in the 8th century; Hindus know it as the residence of the sage Lomas; and Sikhs associate it with Guru Gobind Singh, who camped here in 1705. Three monasteries (Tibetan Buddhist), a gurudwara, and several Hindu temples ring the lake shore. The floating reed islands on the lake surface are analogous to those at Prashar. Rewalsar is reached by a good road 23 km south of Mandi.

The temple is reached by a 3–4 hour trek through dense deodar forest from Khanag village, or by a rough road passable in summer. sundernagar.description: The largest sub-divisional town of Mandi district, Sundernagar at 1,155 m on the Satluj sits above the Sukh Sagar Lake — a reservoir of the Beas-Satluj Link Project that has created a significant water body in the Mandi lowlands. The town has a college, a government hospital and a busy market, and serves as the practical hub for lower Mandi district travel. sections.overview: Shimla, the state capital, served as the summer capital of British India from 1864. The district blends Victorian architecture — the Viceregal Lodge, Christ Church, Gaiety Theatre — with dense cedar and rhododendron forests. Beyond the city, Shimla district offers Narkanda for skiing, Rampur for tribal culture, Chail for the world's highest cricket ground, and Rohru for off-the-beaten-path apple orchards.

chail.description: The Chail hill station, split between Solan and Shimla districts, was created in 1891 by Maharaja Bhupinder Singh of Patiala after the British banned him from Shimla following a dispute. Determined to create a retreat superior to the summer capital, he acquired 5,500 acres of forest on the Shivalik ridge and built the Chail Palace at 2,250 m — now a heritage hotel managed by the Himachal Tourism Corporation. The palace grounds contain the Chail Cricket Ground, built in 1893 at 2,444 m and Guinness-certified as the world's highest playing cricket ground, which still hosts matches. The extensive forest sanctuary surrounding the palace complex contains pheasants, barking deer and leopard.

dadahu.description: A small market village on the Giri Ganga river in central Sirmour, Dadahu is primarily visited as a river camping base — the Giri Ganga in this section runs clear and swift through a forested gorge that is good for nature walks and seasonal fishing. The surrounding oak forest supports leopard, barking deer and a variety of woodland birds. The October–March period, when the weather is mild and clear and the forest is dry, is ideal for camp-based exploration. Basic accommodation is available in the village; most visitors camp on the river flats.
dadahu.name: Dadahu

The village has a small bazaar, a primary health centre and basic guesthouses that fill with pilgrims in the summer trekking season. The ridge viewpoints above the village, accessible on shorter walks, offer views toward both the Shimla hills and the Sirmour plains.
haripurdhar.name: Haripurdhar

nahan.description: Founded in 1621 by Raja Karam Prakash of the Sirmour kingdom on a commanding ridge at 932 m, Nahan is one of Himachal Pradesh's finest examples of a planned hill town — its street grid, central market square and palace complex were laid out in a single design that remains largely intact. The Rani Tal Garden, created by a Sirmour queen in the 19th century as a private pleasure garden, is now a public park of great charm. The Jagannath temple complex on the town ridge has been an active pilgrimage site for four centuries. Nahan's October–March climate — mild days and cool nights, minimal rainfall — makes it the most comfortable lowland town in Himachal and an underrated base for exploring southern Sirmour.
nahan.name: Nahan

paonta_sahib.description: On the west bank of the Yamuna river at the Himachal Pradesh–Uttarakhand border, Paonta Sahib ranks among the most significant Sikh historical sites — the gurdwara marks the place where Guru Gobind Singh, the 10th Sikh Guru, lived from 1685 to 1689 and composed much of his literary work including the Dasam Granth. The Langar (free community kitchen) at the gurdwara feeds thousands daily. The Yamuna at Paonta Sahib is broad and calm in comparison to its upper reaches, and the riverside setting is pleasant. The town is a significant pharmaceutical manufacturing centre — the 'pharma valley' around Paonta Sahib is among India's larger drug manufacturing clusters, a fact that gives the district an unusual economic character.
paonta_sahib.name: Paonta Sahib

rajgarh.description: The Pabbar river valley between Rohru (Shimla district) and the Sirmour border passes through Rajgarh — a small administrative centre at approximately 1,600 m that is the commercial hub for the apple orchards filling this section of the valley. The Pabbar here is an excellent brown trout fishery with a Forest Department permit system. The valley landscape in October, with the apple harvest underway and the surrounding deciduous trees turning colour, is exceptionally scenic and almost entirely unvisited by tourists. A road connects Rajgarh across the watershed to Renuka Lake (approximately 60 km), making a circuit possible for those with their own vehicle.
rajgarh.name: Rajgarh

renuka_lake.description: The largest natural lake in Himachal Pradesh at 3,214 m length and up to 672 m width, Renuka is shaped like the reclining form of the goddess Renuka — the mother of the warrior-sage Parashurama — and this resemblance is the source of its sacred identity. A smaller lake adjacent to the main body is said to be Parashurama himself, watching over his mother. The annual Renuka Fair (November–December, at the Kartik Purnima full moon) is one of Himachal's most important religious gatherings, drawing over 200,000 pilgrims over five days. The lakeside has a modest zoo with a lion, tiger and leopard enclosure, a boating facility, and walking paths. The surrounding forest is habitat for leopard and sloth bear.
renuka_lake.name: Renuka Lake

sarahan_(sirmour).description: Not to be confused with the more famous Sarahan in Kinnaur, this Sarahan in Sirmour district is a small village on the Girri river where the ancient Trilokpur Mata temple draws devotees from across the Shivalik foothills. The temple, set in a forested gorge, is an important local pilgrimage centre for Sirmour's Hindu communities. The Girri valley here is typical of the lower Sirmour landscape — narrow, humid and forested with subtropical species including bamboo and wild banana at lower elevations. This area is undeveloped for tourism and largely visited by pilgrims rather than travellers.
sarahan_(sirmour).name: Sarahan (Sirmour)

shillai.description: On the Uttarakhand border at the southeastern tip of Sirmour district, Shillai is a remote sub-divisional headquarters in a landscape of dense oak and rhododendron forest that is among the least-visited terrain in Himachal Pradesh. The terrain here transitions from the Himalayan foothills to the outer Garhwal ranges, and the forest is remarkably intact — leopard, goral, barking deer and the sloth bear are all present. The spring wildflower display (March–May) in the oak and rhododendron forest below the ridge is spectacular and entirely undiscovered by tourism. Shillai can be reached on a road from Paonta Sahib (approximately 90 km) through continuous forest — the journey itself is as rewarding as the destination.
shillai.name: Shillai

suketi_fossil_park.description: Asia's first fossil park, established in 1974 at Suketi on the banks of the Markanda river, preserves evidence of the extraordinary Shivalik fossil fauna that inhabited this region between 5 and 8 million years ago when the foothills were open woodland and savannah. Life-size concrete replicas of Stegodon (an ancient elephant relative), Sivatherium (a giant giraffe), the Shivalik hippopotamus and a Sivapithecus primate are displayed at the sites where their original fossils were excavated. The adjoining fossil museum contains actual specimens including a complete Stegodon skull. The landscape along the Markanda here is representative of the lower Shivalik — gravel river bars, scrub forest and the red-and-buff Siwalik geological formations.
suketi_fossil_park.name: Suketi Fossil Park

sections.overview: Solan is Himachal's smallest but most industrialised district, closest to Chandigarh. Kasauli is a pristine British-era cantonment — one of India's best-preserved colonial hill stations. The Kasauli Brewery (1820) is Asia's oldest functioning brewery, still producing beer using original methods. Solan is also often described as the 'Mushroom City of India' for its large-scale cultivation. Chail is shared between Solan and Shimla.

barog.description: Barog Station at 1,560 m on the Kalka-Shimla Railway is associated with one of India's most unusual engineering ghost stories: the British engineer Colonel Barog miscalculated the alignment for the tunnel being named after him, resulting in the two ends failing to meet. Disgraced, he died by suicide at the site, and the railway was rerouted through a corrected tunnel design. The station that bears his name is now a popular halt for toy train passengers — the forest rest house adjacent to the platform ranks among the most atmospheric heritage accommodation options on the line. The surrounding Silver Fir Forest (Chil Van) is excellent for birdwatching, with Himalayan woodpeckers, nuthatches and minivets resident throughout the year.
barog.name: Barog

chail.description: The Chail hill station, split between Solan and Shimla districts, was created in 1891 by Maharaja Bhupinder Singh of Patiala after the British banned him from Shimla following a dispute. Determined to create a retreat superior to the summer capital, he acquired 5,500 acres of forest on the Shivalik ridge and built the Chail Palace at 2,250 m — now a heritage hotel managed by the Himachal Tourism Corporation. The palace grounds contain the Chail Cricket Ground, built in 1893 at 2,444 m and Guinness-certified as the world's highest playing cricket ground, which still hosts matches. The extensive forest sanctuary surrounding the palace complex contains pheasants, barking deer and leopard.
chail.name: Chail

dagshai.description: The Dagshai Cantonment, established in 1847 in the Shivalik foothills at 1,830 m, holds a darker chapter of colonial history: the Dagshai prison held British soldiers convicted of mutiny and Irish political prisoners in the late 19th century. The cantonment jail, now converted to a military heritage museum (accessible with permission), documents this little-known history. The stone church, cemetery and garrison buildings are scenicly maintained. The surrounding deodar forest contains several Himalayan bird species, and the ridge trail offers views toward both the Kasauli ridge and the Shimla hills. Dagshai sees very few visitors beyond cantonment residents and military historians.
dagshai.name: Dagshai

kandaghat.description: The Kandaghat station on the UNESCO-listed Kalka-Shimla narrow-gauge railway ranks among the most scenically situated stops on the line — a forest clearing at 1,400 m where the train slows to allow passengers a view of a small waterfall and the oak and rhododendron forest. The nearby area is increasingly known for weekend farmstays and orchards. The Ashwini Khud nature trail beginning near the station follows a seasonal stream through mixed forest for 3 km, making it a good short walk for day visitors arriving by toy train. The Kandaghat–Solan road offers a pleasant cycling route through settled Himachali villages.
kandaghat.name: Kandaghat

kasauli.description: Established in 1842 as a British military sanitarium, Kasauli is among the best-preserved hill cantonments in India — a living museum of colonial Himachal where the architecture, the tree-lined lanes and even the pace of life seem largely unchanged from the late Victorian era. The Kasauli Cantonment Board maintains strict rules: no vehicles are permitted in the inner Mall area, no new construction can exceed the old style, and the original colonial bungalows must be maintained. Monkey Point at the cantonment's southern tip (2,455 m), accessible on foot or in a cantonment vehicle, offers the finest long-range view of the Shivalik foothills and the Punjab plains extending to the horizon. The Pasteur Institute, established in 1900 and still producing anti-rabies vaccine, is one of the cantonment's most historically significant institutions.
kasauli.name: Kasauli

kasauli_brewery.description: The Kasauli Brewery, established by Edward Abraham Dyer in 1820, is the oldest continuously operating brewery in Asia — predating Dyer's better-known Murree Brewery by 35 years. Dyer came to Kasauli specifically because the Himalayan spring water and the cool climate were ideal for lager production, and the springs he identified still supply the brewery today. The site, now owned by Mohan Meakin, produces the Solan No.1 lager brand in the original 1820 stone buildings. Guided tours (bookable in advance) take visitors through the Victorian-era fermenting rooms, conditioning cellars and bottling hall — among the most atmospheric industrial heritage experiences in northern India. The brewery is technically within the cantonment and operating day permits are required.
kasauli_brewery.name: Kasauli Brewery

kumarhatti.description: On the old Hindustan-Tibet Road between Solan and Shimla, Kumarhatti at 1,400 m is a pleasant wayside settlement with government-run horticultural nurseries and experimental orchards that supply grafted apple, peach and apricot stock to farmers across Himachal. The gardens are open to visitors and display an impressive range of temperate fruit varieties and ornamental species. The Kandaghat valley below Kumarhatti, with the Ashwini Khud stream flowing through terraced farmland, is a quiet pastoral landscape suitable for half-day walks. The Kalka-Shimla toy train stops at Kumarhatti station, making it a good base for a day trip on the railway.

shoolini_temple.description: The principal deity of Solan town, Goddess Shoolini is worshipped on a hilltop temple accessible via a 1 km path (or new ropeway) from the main bazaar. The annual Shoolini Mela in June is the district's major cultural event, a three-day celebration that includes folk performances, crafts markets and religious processions drawing tens of thousands of participants. The temple hilltop offers a panoramic view of the Solan valley, the Kasauli ridge, and on clear winter days the plains of Haryana. A smaller shrine to Durga Mata adjacent to the main temple is considered particularly efficacious by local devotees.

solan_town.description: At 1,467 m on the Kalka-Shimla road and railway, Solan is the district headquarters and the largest market town in the region. The Shoolini Mata temple on the ridge above town, accessible by a 1 km path, is the presiding deity of the town and the site of the annual Shoolini Mela (June). Solan's claim to the title 'Mushroom City of India' is well-founded: the Solan Mushroom Research Centre (established 1961) pioneered commercial mushroom cultivation in India, and button mushroom farms dot the hillsides around the town. The town also sits within the Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh pharmaceutical and industrial belt, Himachal's largest industrial zone.

subathu.description: At 1,200 m in the Shivalik foothills, Subathu holds the distinction of being one of the oldest British military cantonments in northern India, established in 1815 immediately after the Anglo-Gurkha War. The Gurkha Regimental Centre has been headquartered here since that date, making Subathu an important institution in the history of the Indian Army. The cantonment church (St. Andrew's, 1835), the officers' mess and the regimental museum are architectural and historical landmarks. The surrounding secondary forest has good birdwatching. Subathu is 45 km from Shimla on the old hill road and sees almost no tourism.
subathu.name: Subathu

Solan is also often described as the 'Mushroom City of India' for its large-scale cultivation. Chail is shared between Solan and Shimla.

The surrounding Silver Fir Forest (Chil Van) is excellent for birdwatching, with Himalayan woodpeckers, nuthatches and minivets resident throughout the year.
